### A guided tour of Fermat–Weber geometry, told through six stubborn measurements

---

## 1. A question with money attached

Imagine an experiment that has to answer a single practical question: *how much can we throw away before quality breaks?* You sweep a budget $k$ upward, you watch a quality ratio $q(k)$ climb, and you record the smallest $k$ at which $q(k)$ clears a fixed bar. That number is the **knee**, $k^\*$. It is the deployable budget, and every unit you shave off it is speed you keep.

The trouble is that $k^\*$ is noisy. Repeat the experiment with a different random seed and you get a different number. At context length $2048$, three repetitions gave

$$k^\* \in \{160,\ 224,\ 256\}.$$

Before the last of those runs, four specific point predictions were recorded: $224$, $240$, $256$, $192$. The measurement came in at $160$. **All four were refuted.**

And yet one claim survived — a claim not about any single run, but about the *centre* of the distribution:

$$\operatorname{median}\{160,\,224,\,256\} \;=\; 224 \;=\; \tfrac{7}{8}\cdot 256 .$$

Here $256 = d\cdot\mathrm{ctx}/32$ is the natural **product point** of the experiment. At the shorter context $\mathrm{ctx}=1024$, with product point $128$, three earlier repetitions gave $\{96,112,128\}$ with median $112 = \tfrac78\cdot 128$. Same constant. Six measurements, two contexts, one number.

> **The question this page answers:** why is the centre predictable when the measurements are not? The answer is geometric, and it is sharp enough to tell you in advance exactly how much abuse the centre can absorb.

---

## 2. First, play with it

Everything below is a consequence of one picture. So look at the picture before reading the theory.

The curve is the **total distance**
$$F(t) \;=\; \sum_i |t - x_i|,$$
plotted as you move a candidate centre $t$ along the line. Drag the measurements. Toggle the fourth one on and off. Notice two things and you will have discovered the entire subject:

* with an **odd** number of measurements the curve has a single lowest point, and it is the middle measurement;
* with an **even** number of measurements the curve has a flat bottom — a whole **segment** of equally optimal centres.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

<details>
<summary><b>What is the shaded band, exactly?</b></summary>

It is the set of minimisers of $F$. The function $F$ is piecewise linear, with a kink at every measurement; its slope at $t$ is $\#\{x_i < t\} - \#\{x_i > t\}$. So the slope is negative while the majority of data lies above $t$, positive once the majority lies below, and zero on any stretch where the two counts agree. The flat bottom is exactly that stretch — which is why it is a point in odd size (the counts can never tie) and a segment in even size (they can).
</details>

---

## 3. The oldest definition of "middle"

Most of us meet the median as a sorting recipe. There is an older definition, and it is the one that has geometry in it.

> **Definition.** The **Fermat–Weber point** (or *geometric median*) of points $p_1,\dots,p_n$ is the location minimising the total distance $\sum_i \operatorname{dist}(t,p_i)$.

Fermat posed it for three points in the plane; the economist Alfred Weber used it to site a factory optimally among its suppliers. On a line, the Fermat–Weber point and the sorted-list median coincide — and that coincidence is precisely what makes the median robust.

Here is the three-point theorem, in the cleanest generality it admits.

> **Theorem (betweenness points are geometric medians).** In *any* metric space, if $q$ lies metrically between $p$ and $r$ — meaning $d(p,q) + d(q,r) = d(p,r)$ — then for every point $x$,
> $$d(x,p) + d(x,q) + d(x,r) \;\ge\; d(p,r),$$
> with equality **if and only if** $x = q$.

<details>
<summary><b>Click for the two-line proof</b></summary>

The triangle inequality gives $d(p,r) \le d(x,p) + d(x,r)$. Adding $d(x,q)$ to both sides,
$$d(p,r) + d(x,q) \;\le\; d(x,p) + d(x,q) + d(x,r).$$
So the total is at least $d(p,r)$, and equality forces $d(x,q) = 0$, i.e. $x = q$. Conversely, at $x=q$ the total is $d(q,p) + 0 + d(q,r) = d(p,r)$ by betweenness. $\blacksquare$

No convexity, no derivatives, no ordering — just one triangle inequality. That is why the same statement specialises to the real line ($|x-a|+|x-b|+|x-c| \ge c-a$ with equality iff $x=b$) *and* to three collinear points in any normed space, where it says the geometric median does not wander off the line into the ambient space.
</details>

Applied to the data: for every $x$,
$$|x-160| + |x-224| + |x-256| \;\ge\; 96, \qquad\text{equality iff } x = 224,$$
$$|x-96| + |x-112| + |x-128| \;\ge\; 32, \qquad\text{equality iff } x = 112.$$

So the "$7/8$ law" is not an artefact of sorting. It is a **variational** statement: $\tfrac78$ of the product point is the location that minimises total distance to the measurements, at both contexts.

{{visualization:0}}

## 4. The complete rule: balance

The three-point argument stops working the moment the sample size changes parity, so we need the general law. It turns out to be a pure counting condition — no arithmetic on the data at all.

> **Definition.** A point $m$ is **balanced** for a sample $S$ if neither open side outweighs the other:
> $$\#\{x > m\} \le \#\{x \le m\} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \#\{x < m\} \le \#\{x \ge m\}.$$

> **Theorem (characterisation).** $m$ minimises the total distance to $S$ **if and only if** $m$ is balanced for $S$.

<details>
<summary><b>Click for the proof of sufficiency (a counting argument, valid far beyond the real line)</b></summary>

Suppose $m$ is balanced and $m \le t$. For each datum $x$,
$$|m - x| \;+\; \begin{cases} t - m, & x \le m \\ -(t-m), & x > m \end{cases} \;\le\; |t-x| ,$$
with equality in the first case (both absolute values open the same way) and the inequality $-(t-x) \le |t-x|$ in the second. Summing over the sample and grouping the two-valued term by counts,
$$F(m) + \#\{x\le m\}\,(t-m) - \#\{x>m\}\,(t-m) \;\le\; F(t).$$
Balance says $\#\{x>m\} \le \#\{x\le m\}$, so the middle terms are $\ge 0$ and $F(m) \le F(t)$. The other direction of travel is symmetric. Notice what the proof never used: completeness, division, or even real numbers. It works in any linearly ordered abelian group. $\blacksquare$
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Click for the proof of necessity (a finitary witness — no limits)</b></summary>

Suppose the sample is strictly heavier above $m$: $\#\{x\le m\} < \#\{x>m\}$. Let $t$ be the **nearest** datum above $m$. Because the step from $m$ to $t$ jumps over no data, every absolute value keeps its sign, and the cost changes *exactly* linearly:
$$F(t) = F(m) + \bigl(\#\{x\le m\} - \#\{x>m\}\bigr)(t-m) \;<\; F(m).$$
So $m$ was not optimal. The witness is a data point, so nothing continuous or asymptotic enters the argument. $\blacksquare$
</details>

The balance test is an **optimality certificate you can compute in one pass**, comparing only counts:

{{algorithm:1}}

And for odd samples the count gap is at least one, which upgrades minimality into a *sharp slope bound*: for a sample of size $2k+1$ with counting median $m$,
$$F(m) + |t - m| \;\le\; F(t).$$
The cost rises at unit rate, at least, as you leave the median — so the median is not merely a minimum, it is a *corner*, and it is unique.

Because $F$ is convex (a pointwise consequence of the triangle inequality), the set of minimisers is convex, hence an interval. Odd samples: a point. Even samples: a segment. Which brings us to the algorithm that reads it straight off the order statistics:

## 5. Why the centre is *robust*: it is a projection

Here is the mechanism. Freeze two measurements, let the third vary, and ask what the median does as a function of the free one. The answer is startlingly clean:

$$\operatorname{med}(a,b,x) \;=\; \max\Bigl(\min(a,b),\ \min\bigl(\max(a,b),\, x\bigr)\Bigr).$$

In words: **clamp $x$ to the segment spanned by $a$ and $b$**. The median of three is the nearest-point projection of the free measurement onto the interval fixed by the other two.

Four consequences, all visible in the widget above:

1. **The centre can never escape.** A projection lands in its target set, so no third measurement, however wild, can push the median outside $[a\wedge b,\ a\vee b]$ — and its range is exactly that compact segment.
2. **Excursions are absorbed.** Projections are $1$-Lipschitz, and better: **firmly nonexpansive**,
 $$\bigl(P(x)-P(y)\bigr)^2 \;\le\; (x-y)\bigl(P(x)-P(y)\bigr).$$
 A displacement of the input is never merely bounded in the output — it is contracted against its own direction.
3. **Stability is a half-line, not a tolerance.** The fibre of a projection over an *endpoint* is a closed half-line (the segment's [normal cone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_cone) there); over an *interior* point it is a single point. For the measured data, the third measurements leaving the centre at $224$ are exactly those with $x \le 224$ — an unbounded set.
4. **The mean has none of this.** With two measurements fixed, the arithmetic mean is a surjection onto $\mathbb{R}$: one wild value drags it anywhere. On the measured triple it is $640/3 \approx 213.33$, which is not $224$ and is not $7/8$ of anything.

## 6. Two contexts, two rays, and one stubborn defect

Now compare the contexts. Plot every measurement as a point $(\mathrm{ctx}, k^\*)$ in the plane. Two points lie on a common ray through the origin exactly when the determinant $x_1y_2 - y_1x_2$ vanishes.

{{visualization:1}}

* **The top edge is a ray.** $(1024,128)$ and $(2048,256)$: slope $1/8$, determinant $0$. The product-point law $k^\* \le d\cdot\mathrm{ctx}/32$ is exact proportionality — and every one of the six measurements respects it.
* **The median is a ray too.** $(1024,112)$ and $(2048,224)$: slope $\tfrac{7}{64} = \tfrac78\cdot\tfrac18$, the product slope scaled by the law constant. And this is a genuine test rather than a double fit: a proportional law matching the short context is *forced* to have slope $7/64$, with no freedom left, and that slope then hits the long context exactly.
* **The low tail is not a ray.** $(1024,96)$ and $(2048,160)$: determinant $-32768$, origin triangle of area $16384$. No proportional law fits it.

Doubling the context is the dilation $p \mapsto 2p$. It carries the top point and the median point to their long-context counterparts — the law is *equivariant*. It fails on the low tail by exactly
$$2\cdot 96 - 160 \;=\; 32 \;=\; \frac{256}{8} \;=\; \frac{P}{8},$$
and no dilation whatsoever matches the whole configuration (the top edge demands factor $2$, the low tail demands $5/3$).

**So the knee distribution is not self-similar, even though its centre and its upper edge are — and all of the non-self-similarity is one scalar.**

$$\tfrac38 \;=\; \tfrac32\cdot\tfrac14 .$$
The reported "roughly $50\%$ wider" is exact. Moreover the widening is **entirely** a low-tail phenomenon: the top two normalised coordinates are identical at both contexts, and the cost increase $\tfrac38 - \tfrac14 = \tfrac18$ equals precisely the drop in the low coordinate, $\tfrac34 - \tfrac58 = \tfrac18$.

Treat the normalised triples as points of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and look at the level set $\{\operatorname{med} = 7/8\}$. Both measurements lie in it, but so does the entire segment joining them — because the whole half-line $\{(t,\,7/8,\,1) : t\le 7/8\}$ lies in the level set. The low coordinate is invisible to the centre so long as it stays below it, and the half-line is **maximal**: as soon as $t$ exceeds $7/8$, $\operatorname{med}(t,7/8,1) = t$ and the centre moves.

Why is that not automatic? Because the level set is **not convex**. The triples $(5/8,\,7/8,\,1)$ and $(7/8,\,1,\,5/8)$ both have median $7/8$, but their midpoint $(3/4,\,15/16,\,13/16)$ has median $13/16$. Two points can each have the right centre while everything between them does not. That the two measured contexts lie in a *common flat face* of this crooked set is information about the data.

## 7. The prediction that cannot fail — and why that is useful

The next experiment adds a **fourth** measurement at the long context. Parity flips, and the optimum becomes a segment. Here is the entire prediction, stated before the run.

> **Theorem.** Let $x$ be the fourth measured value, whatever it turns out to be. Then $224$ is an optimal centre of $\{160,224,256,x\}$, and the optimal cost is exactly
> $$96 + |224 - x| .$$
> If $x \in [160,224]$ the optimal set is $[x, 224]$ — it widens *downwards*, with its upper endpoint pinned at the centre. If $x \in [224,256]$ it is $[224, x]$ — widening upwards, lower endpoint pinned. The optimum is a *unique* point only in the knife-edge case $x = 224$.

<details>
<summary><b>Click for the proof (again, two triangle inequalities)</b></summary>

For any $t$:
$$|t-160| + |t-256| \;\ge\; 256 - 160 = 96, \qquad |t-224| + |t-x| \;\ge\; |224 - x| .$$
Adding gives $F(t) \ge 96 + |224-x|$, and at $t = 224$ both are tight, since $|224-160| + |224-256| = 64+32 = 96$ and $|224-224| + |224-x| = |224-x|$. So the bound is attained at $224$ for every $x$. The regime statements are the four-point equality criterion applied to the sorted data. $\blacksquare$

Equivalently, and more structurally: $224$ is **balanced** for $\{160,224,256,y\}$ for every $y$ — if $y \le 224$ then three of the four entries lie at or below $224$ and two lie at or above; otherwise two lie on each side. Balance is optimality, so the conclusion is immediate from the general characterisation.
</details>

Set the fourth slider anywhere in the widget above and watch it: the shaded band grows and shrinks, but one of its endpoints never leaves $224$.

**A prediction that cannot be refuted is usually a bad one — and here that is exactly the finding.** It tells the experimenters that the fourth measurement is not a test of the centre at all. The centre is protected by the geometry. What the fourth run actually tests is the *low tail*: whether the value $160$, and the ratio $5/8$ it represents, is a stable feature of the long context or an accident of one seed. Stated in the right variational language, the quantity to watch is the **lower endpoint of the optimal segment**.

## 9. The moral, in one paragraph

Four point predictions failed and one structural prediction held, and the difference was not luck. A single measurement is a grid-quantised crossing of a noisy curve — the last one cleared the bar by $+0.0012$, so the true threshold sits somewhere around $150$–$160$, invisible between grid points. /-! ## The four-point Fermat–Weber problem -/

/-- Total distance from `t` to a four-point sample. -/
def cost4 (a b c d t : ℝ) : ℝ := |t - a| + |t - b| + |t - c| + |t - d|

/-- **Lower bound for an even sample.**  For sorted data the total distance is at least the
sum of the two nested spreads `(d - a) + (c - b)`. -/
theorem fermatWeber_four {a b c d : ℝ} (hab : a ≤ b) (hbc : b ≤ c) (hcd : c ≤ d) (t : ℝ) :
    (d - a) + (c - b) ≤ cost4 a b c d t := by
  have h1 : d - a ≤ |t - a| + |t - d| := by
    rcases abs_cases (t - a) with ⟨h, _⟩ | ⟨h, _⟩ <;>
      rcases abs_cases (t - d) with ⟨h', _⟩ | ⟨h', _⟩ <;> linarith
  have h2 : c - b ≤ |t - b| + |t - c| := by
    rcases abs_cases (t - b) with ⟨h, _⟩ | ⟨h, _⟩ <;>
      rcases abs_cases (t - c) with ⟨h', _⟩ | ⟨h', _⟩ <;> linarith
  simp only [cost4]
  linarith

    (t : ℝ) : cost4 a b c d t = (d - a) + (c - b) ↔ b ≤ t ∧ t ≤ c := by
  constructor
  · intro h
    simp only [cost4] at h
    constructor
    · by_contra ht
      push_neg at ht
      have h1 : |t - a| + |t - d| ≥ d - a := by
        rcases abs_cases (t - a) with ⟨h', _⟩ | ⟨h', _⟩ <;>
          rcases abs_cases (t - d) with ⟨h'', _⟩ | ⟨h'', _⟩ <;> linarith
      have h2 : |t - b| = b - t := by
        rw [abs_of_nonpos (by linarith)]; ring
      have h3 : |t - c| = c - t := by
        rw [abs_of_nonpos (by linarith)]; ring
      rw [h2, h3] at h
      linarith
    · by_contra ht
      push_neg at ht
      have h1 : |t - a| + |t - d| ≥ d - a := by
        rcases abs_cases (t - a) with ⟨h', _⟩ | ⟨h', _⟩ <;>
          rcases abs_cases (t - d) with ⟨h'', _⟩ | ⟨h'', _⟩ <;> linarith
      have h2 : |t - b| = t - b := by
        rw [abs_of_nonneg (by linarith)]
      have h3 : |t - c| = t - c := by
        rw [abs_of_nonneg (by linarith)]
      rw [h2, h3] at h
      linarith

    simp only [cost4]
    rw [abs_of_nonneg (by linarith : (0:ℝ) ≤ t - a), abs_of_nonneg (by linarith : (0:ℝ) ≤ t - b),

the two middle order statistics coincide. -/
theorem fermatWeber_four_unique_iff {a b c d : ℝ} (hab : a ≤ b) (hbc : b ≤ c) (hcd : c ≤ d) :

  · intro h
    have := h c ((fermatWeber_four_eq_iff hab hbc hcd c).mpr ⟨hbc, le_refl c⟩)
    exact this.symm
  · rintro rfl
    intro t ht
    exact le_antisymm ((fermatWeber_four_eq_iff hab hbc hcd t).mp ht).2

`Geometry.FermatWeberMedian` shows that a counting median of an **odd** sample minimises the

supplies the general theory, for samples of arbitrary size and parity:

    `m` minimises `fwCost s`  ⟺  `m` is **balanced**: at least half of the sample lies weakly

set is an interval — a point for odd samples, a genuine segment for even ones.

* `IsBalanced` — the counting condition `#{x > m} ≤ #{x ≤ m}` and `#{x < m} ≤ #{x ≥ m}`.

  point minimises the total distance.
* `IsMedian.isBalanced` — the counting median of an odd sample is balanced, so the odd theorem
  of `FermatWeberMedian` is the odd case of this one.
* `isBalanced_of_min` — **necessity**, over `ℝ`: a minimiser is balanced.  The witness is the
  nearest sample point on the heavy side, so the argument is genuinely finitary; no limiting
  argument is used.
* `fwCost_min_iff_isBalanced` — the characterisation.
* `fwCost_convex` — convexity of the cost functional, proved pointwise from the triangle

* `minimiser_set_convex` — consequently the set of Fermat–Weber points is convex: an interval.
  This is the structural reason why a fourth seed can only *widen* the optimal centre into a
  segment rather than move it.

other: at least as many entries are `≤ m` as are `> m`, and at least as many are `≥ m` as are
`< m`. -/
def IsBalanced (s : Multiset α) (m : α) : Prop :=
  card (s.filter (fun x => ¬ x ≤ m)) ≤ card (s.filter (fun x => x ≤ m)) ∧
    card (s.filter (fun x => ¬ m ≤ x)) ≤ card (s.filter (fun x => m ≤ x))

        push_neg at hx

        have hrw : m - x + -(m - t) = t - x := by abel
        rw [hrw]
        exact le_abs_self _
    have hsum := Multiset.sum_map_le_sum_map
      (fun x : α => |m - x| + (if m ≤ x then m - t else -(m - t)))
      (fun x : α => |t - x|) hpt
    rw [Multiset.sum_map_add, sum_map_ite_const] at hsum
    have hmcost : (s.map (fun x : α => |m - x|)).sum = fwCost s m := rfl
    rw [hmcost] at hsum

      obtain ⟨r, hr⟩ : ∃ r : ℕ, A = C + r := ⟨A - C, by omega⟩
      rw [hr, add_nsmul]

        rw [← nsmul_add]; simp

          = (C • (m - t) + C • (-(m - t))) + r • (m - t) := by abel
      rw [hrearr, hCneg, zero_add]

/-! ## Necessity, over the reals -/

/-- Exact cost of a step to the right that jumps no sample point. -/
theorem fwCost_step_right {s : Multiset ℝ} {m t : ℝ} (hmt : m ≤ t)
    (hgap : ∀ x ∈ s, m < x → t ≤ x) :
    fwCost s t = fwCost s m
      + ((card (s.filter (fun x => x ≤ m)) : ℝ) - (card (s.filter (fun x => ¬ x ≤ m)) : ℝ))
        * (t - m) := by
  classical
  have hpt : ∀ x ∈ s, |t - x| = |m - x| + (if x ≤ m then t - m else -(t - m)) := by
    intro x hx
    by_cases hxm : x ≤ m
    · rw [if_pos hxm, abs_of_nonneg (by linarith), abs_of_nonneg (by linarith)]
      ring
    · push_neg at hxm
      have htx : t ≤ x := hgap x hx hxm
      rw [if_neg (not_le.mpr hxm), abs_of_nonpos (by linarith), abs_of_nonpos (by linarith)]
      ring
  have hmap : (s.map (fun x : ℝ => |t - x|)).sum
      = (s.map (fun x : ℝ => |m - x| + (if x ≤ m then t - m else -(t - m)))).sum := by
    rw [Multiset.map_congr rfl hpt]
  have : fwCost s t = (s.map (fun x : ℝ => |t - x|)).sum := rfl
  rw [this, hmap, Multiset.sum_map_add, sum_map_ite_const]
  have hmcost : (s.map (fun x : ℝ => |m - x|)).sum = fwCost s m := rfl
  rw [hmcost, nsmul_eq_mul, nsmul_eq_mul]
  ring

/-- Exact cost of a step to the left that jumps no sample point. -/
theorem fwCost_step_left {s : Multiset ℝ} {m t : ℝ} (htm : t ≤ m)
    (hgap : ∀ x ∈ s, x < m → x ≤ t) :
    fwCost s t = fwCost s m
      + ((card (s.filter (fun x => m ≤ x)) : ℝ) - (card (s.filter (fun x => ¬ m ≤ x)) : ℝ))
        * (m - t) := by
  classical
  have hpt : ∀ x ∈ s, |t - x| = |m - x| + (if m ≤ x then m - t else -(m - t)) := by
    intro x hx
    by_cases hxm : m ≤ x
    · rw [if_pos hxm, abs_of_nonpos (by linarith), abs_of_nonpos (by linarith)]
      ring
    · push_neg at hxm
      have hxt : x ≤ t := hgap x hx hxm
      rw [if_neg (not_le.mpr hxm), abs_of_nonneg (by linarith), abs_of_nonneg (by linarith)]
      ring
  have hmap : (s.map (fun x : ℝ => |t - x|)).sum
      = (s.map (fun x : ℝ => |m - x| + (if m ≤ x then m - t else -(m - t)))).sum := by
    rw [Multiset.map_congr rfl hpt]
  have : fwCost s t = (s.map (fun x : ℝ => |t - x|)).sum := rfl
  rw [this, hmap, Multiset.sum_map_add, sum_map_ite_const]
  have hmcost : (s.map (fun x : ℝ => |m - x|)).sum = fwCost s m := rfl
  rw [hmcost, nsmul_eq_mul, nsmul_eq_mul]
  ring

/-- **Necessity.**  A minimiser of the total distance is balanced.  The witness step is to the
nearest sample point on the heavier side, so the argument is finitary. -/
theorem isBalanced_of_min {s : Multiset ℝ} {m : ℝ} (hmin : ∀ t, fwCost s m ≤ fwCost s t) :
    IsBalanced s m := by
  classical
  constructor
  · by_contra hcon
    set A := card (s.filter (fun x => x ≤ m)) with hA
    set C := card (s.filter (fun x => ¬ x ≤ m)) with hC
    have hlt : A < C := not_le.mp hcon
    have hCpos : 0 < C := lt_of_le_of_lt (Nat.zero_le A) hlt
    have hne : (s.filter (fun x => ¬ x ≤ m)).toFinset.Nonempty := by
      obtain ⟨y, hy⟩ := Multiset.card_pos_iff_exists_mem.mp hCpos
      exact ⟨y, Multiset.mem_toFinset.mpr hy⟩
    set t := (s.filter (fun x => ¬ x ≤ m)).toFinset.min' hne with ht
    have htmem : t ∈ s.filter (fun x => ¬ x ≤ m) := by
      have := Finset.min'_mem _ hne
      rwa [Multiset.mem_toFinset] at this
    have htgt : m < t := by
      have := (Multiset.mem_filter.mp htmem).2
      exact not_le.mp this
    have hgap : ∀ x ∈ s, m < x → t ≤ x := by
      intro x hx hmx
      have hxmem : x ∈ (s.filter (fun x => ¬ x ≤ m)).toFinset := by
        rw [Multiset.mem_toFinset]
        exact Multiset.mem_filter.mpr ⟨hx, not_le.mpr hmx⟩
      exact Finset.min'_le _ _ hxmem

    have hAC : (A : ℝ) - (C : ℝ) < 0 := by
      have : (A : ℝ) < (C : ℝ) := by exact_mod_cast hlt
      linarith
    have hpos : 0 < t - m := by linarith
    have : fwCost s t < fwCost s m := by
      rw [hstep]
      nlinarith

    set C := card (s.filter (fun x => ¬ m ≤ x)) with hC
    have hlt : A < C := not_le.mp hcon

    have hne : (s.filter (fun x => ¬ m ≤ x)).toFinset.Nonempty := by
      obtain ⟨y, hy⟩ := Multiset.card_pos_iff_exists_mem.mp hCpos

    have htmem : t ∈ s.filter (fun x => ¬ m ≤ x) := by
      have := Finset.max'_mem _ hne
      rwa [Multiset.mem_toFinset] at this
    have htlt : t < m := by
      have := (Multiset.mem_filter.mp htmem).2
      exact not_le.mp this
    have hgap : ∀ x ∈ s, x < m → x ≤ t := by
      intro x hx hxm
      have hxmem : x ∈ (s.filter (fun x => ¬ m ≤ x)).toFinset := by
        rw [Multiset.mem_toFinset]
        exact Multiset.mem_filter.mpr ⟨hx, not_le.mpr hxm⟩
      exact Finset.le_max' _ _ hxmem
    have hstep := fwCost_step_left htlt.le hgap
    have hAC : (A : ℝ) - (C : ℝ) < 0 := by
      have : (A : ℝ) < (C : ℝ) := by exact_mod_cast hlt
      linarith
    have hpos : 0 < m - t := by linarith
    have : fwCost s t < fwCost s m := by
      rw [hstep]
      nlinarith
    exact absurd (hmin t) (not_le.mpr this)

/-- **The characterisation**: over the reals, the Fermat–Weber points of a sample are exactly
its balanced points. -/
theorem fwCost_min_iff_isBalanced {s : Multiset ℝ} {m : ℝ} :
    (∀ t, fwCost s m ≤ fwCost s t) ↔ IsBalanced s m :=
  ⟨isBalanced_of_min, fun h t => fwCost_le_of_isBalanced h t⟩

/-! ## Convexity, and the minimiser set as an interval -/

/-- The total-distance functional is convex. -/
theorem fwCost_convex (s : Multiset ℝ) (a b : ℝ) {l : ℝ} (hl0 : 0 ≤ l) (hl1 : l ≤ 1) :
    fwCost s (l * a + (1 - l) * b) ≤ l * fwCost s a + (1 - l) * fwCost s b := by
  have hpt : ∀ x ∈ s, |l * a + (1 - l) * b - x| ≤ l * |a - x| + (1 - l) * |b - x| := by
    intro x _
    have hrw : l * a + (1 - l) * b - x = l * (a - x) + (1 - l) * (b - x) := by ring
    rw [hrw]
    calc |l * (a - x) + (1 - l) * (b - x)| ≤ |l * (a - x)| + |(1 - l) * (b - x)| :=
          abs_add_le _ _
      _ = l * |a - x| + (1 - l) * |b - x| := by
          rw [abs_mul, abs_mul, abs_of_nonneg hl0, abs_of_nonneg (show (0:ℝ) ≤ 1 - l by linarith)]
  have hsum := Multiset.sum_map_le_sum_map
    (fun x : ℝ => |l * a + (1 - l) * b - x|)
    (fun x : ℝ => l * |a - x| + (1 - l) * |b - x|) hpt
  rw [Multiset.sum_map_add, Multiset.sum_map_mul_left, Multiset.sum_map_mul_left] at hsum
  exact hsum

/-- **The Fermat–Weber set is convex**: if two points both minimise the total distance, so does
every point between them.  For an even sample this is why the optimal centre is a segment. -/
theorem minimiser_set_convex {s : Multiset ℝ} {a b t : ℝ}
    (ha : ∀ u, fwCost s a ≤ fwCost s u) (hb : ∀ u, fwCost s b ≤ fwCost s u)
    (hat : a ≤ t) (htb : t ≤ b) (u : ℝ) : fwCost s t ≤ fwCost s u := by
  rcases eq_or_lt_of_le hat with rfl | halt
  · exact ha u
  · have hab : a < b := lt_of_lt_of_le halt htb
    obtain ⟨l, hl0, hl1, hcomb⟩ : ∃ l : ℝ, 0 ≤ l ∧ l ≤ 1 ∧ l * a + (1 - l) * b = t := by
      have hne' : b - a ≠ 0 := ne_of_gt (by linarith)
      refine ⟨(b - t) / (b - a), div_nonneg (by linarith) (by linarith), ?_, ?_⟩
      · rw [div_le_one (by linarith)]
        linarith
      · field_simp
        ring
    have hcvx := fwCost_convex s a b hl0 hl1
    rw [hcomb] at hcvx
    have hcost : fwCost s a = fwCost s b := le_antisymm (ha b) (hb a)
    rw [hcost] at hcvx
    have hid : l * fwCost s b + (1 - l) * fwCost s b = fwCost s b := by ring
    rw [hid] at hcvx
    exact le_trans hcvx (hb u)

  rcases le_total y 224 with hy | hy <;>
    refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩ <;>

theorem net48_224_min (y t : ℝ) :
    fwCost ({160, 224, 256, y} : Multiset ℝ) 224 ≤ fwCost ({160, 224, 256, y} : Multiset ℝ) t :=
  fwCost_le_of_isBalanced (net48_224_isBalanced y) t

/-- The Fermat–Weber cost (total distance) of a candidate centre `t` against a sample `s`. -/
def fwCost (s : Multiset α) (t : α) : α := (s.map (fun x => |t - x|)).sum

/-- A two-valued sum over a multiset splits according to the filter cardinalities. -/
theorem sum_map_ite_const {β : Type*} [AddCommGroup β] (s : Multiset β) (p : β → Prop)

  | empty => simp

        abel

/-- The two complementary filters of a sample have cardinalities summing to its size. -/
theorem card_filter_add_card_filter_not {β : Type*} (s : Multiset β) (p : β → Prop)
    [DecidablePred p] :
    card (s.filter p) + card (s.filter (fun x => ¬ p x)) = card s := by
  rw [← Multiset.card_add, Multiset.filter_add_not]

theorem fwCost_slope_ge_right {k : ℕ} {s : Multiset α} {m : α} (hcard : card s = 2 * k + 1)

      (fwCost_slope_ge_right hcard h hmt)
  · exact le_trans (le_add_of_nonneg_right (sub_nonneg.mpr htm))
      (fwCost_slope_ge_left hcard h htm)

/-! ## The metric core: a betweenness point is the unique Fermat–Weber point -/

variable {X : Type*} [MetricSpace X]

/-- **Fermat–Weber lower bound.**  In any metric space the total distance from `x` to a
triple `p, q, r` is at least `dist p r + dist x q`.  (Only the triangle inequality is
used; no betweenness hypothesis is needed for this half.) -/
theorem dist_sum_ge (p q r x : X) :
    dist p r + dist x q ≤ dist x p + dist x q + dist x r := by
  have h : dist p r ≤ dist p x + dist x r := dist_triangle p x r
  rw [dist_comm p x] at h
  linarith

/-- If `q` lies metrically between `p` and `r`, the total distance functional at `q`
equals the diameter `dist p r`. -/
theorem fermatWeber_value_at_between {p q r : X}
    (hq : dist p q + dist q r = dist p r) :
    dist q p + dist q q + dist q r = dist p r := by
  rw [dist_self, dist_comm q p]
  linarith

/-- **The Fermat–Weber theorem for a betweenness triple.**  If `q` is between `p` and `r`,
then the total-distance functional is bounded below by `dist p r`, and the bound is
attained at `q`. -/
theorem dist_sum_ge_of_between {p q r : X}
    (hq : dist p q + dist q r = dist p r) (x : X) :
    dist q p + dist q q + dist q r ≤ dist x p + dist x q + dist x r := by
  rw [fermatWeber_value_at_between hq]
  have hq0 : (0:ℝ) ≤ dist x q := dist_nonneg
  linarith [dist_sum_ge p q r x]

the Fermat–Weber bound forces `x = q`. -/
theorem fermatWeber_eq_iff {p q r : X}
    (hq : dist p q + dist q r = dist p r) (x : X) :
    dist x p + dist x q + dist x r = dist p r ↔ x = q := by
  constructor
  · intro hx
    have h := dist_sum_ge p q r x
    have hxq : dist x q ≤ 0 := by linarith
    have : dist x q = 0 := le_antisymm hxq dist_nonneg
    exact dist_eq_zero.mp this
  · rintro rfl
    have := fermatWeber_value_at_between hq
    rw [dist_self] at this ⊢
    rw [dist_comm x p] at this ⊢
    linarith

/-- On the real line, `a ≤ b ≤ c` makes `b` a betweenness point. -/
theorem real_between {a b c : ℝ} (hab : a ≤ b) (hbc : b ≤ c) :
    dist a b + dist b c = dist a c := by
  rw [Real.dist_eq, Real.dist_eq, Real.dist_eq, abs_of_nonpos (by linarith),
    abs_of_nonpos (by linarith), abs_of_nonpos (by linarith)]
  ring

/-- **The median of three reals minimises the sum of absolute deviations**, and the
optimal value is the spread `c - a`. -/
theorem fermatWeber_real {a b c : ℝ} (hab : a ≤ b) (hbc : b ≤ c) (x : ℝ) :
    c - a ≤ |x - a| + |x - b| + |x - c| := by
  have h := dist_sum_ge_of_between (real_between hab hbc) x
  simp only [Real.dist_eq] at h

    abs_of_nonpos (by linarith : b - c ≤ 0)] at h
  linarith

theorem fermatWeber_real_eq_iff {a b c : ℝ} (hab : a ≤ b) (hbc : b ≤ c) (x : ℝ) :

  have h := fermatWeber_eq_iff (real_between hab hbc) x
  simp only [Real.dist_eq] at h
  have habs : c - a = |a - c| := by
    rw [abs_of_nonpos (by linarith : a - c ≤ 0)]; ring
  rw [habs]

theorem fermatWeber_real_eq_tropMed3 {a b c : ℝ} (hab : a ≤ b) (hbc : b ≤ c) (x : ℝ)
    (hx : |x - a| + |x - b| + |x - c| = c - a) : x = tropMed3 a b c := by
  have hb : tropMed3 a b c = b := by
    simp only [tropMed3, min_def, max_def]
    split_ifs <;> order
  rw [hb]

  rw [dist_line v hu, dist_line v hu, dist_line v hu, abs_of_nonpos (by linarith),

  ring

  rw [fermatWeber_value_at_between (collinear_between v hu hab hbc),

def clamp (a b x : α) : α := max (min a b) (min (max a b) x)

theorem tropMed3_eq_proj (a b x : α) : tropMed3 a b x = clamp a b x := by

/-- The projection is monotone in the third seed. -/
theorem proj_monotone (a b : ℝ) {x y : ℝ} (hxy : x ≤ y) :

from typing import Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

# 1. Fermat-Weber cost, minimiser set, and the balance certificate
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def fw_cost(sample: Sequence[Num], t: Num) -> Num:
    """Total distance from the candidate centre `t` to every sample point."""
    return sum((abs(t - x) for x in sample), Fraction(0))


def is_balanced(sample: Sequence[Num], m: Num) -> bool:
    """`m` is balanced: neither open side of `m` holds more than half the sample."""
    n_le = sum(1 for x in sample if x <= m)
    n_lt = sum(1 for x in sample if x < m)
    n = len(sample)
    return (n - n_le) <= n_le and n_lt <= (n - n_lt)


def fermat_weber_set(sample: Sequence[Num]) -> Tuple[Num, Num]:
    """Endpoints of the interval of minimisers of the total distance.

    Odd size 2k+1: the singleton [x_(k+1), x_(k+1)].
    Even size 2k : the middle segment [x_(k), x_(k+1)].

    xs = sorted(sample)
    n = len(xs)
    if n % 2 == 1:
        mid = xs[n // 2]
        return (mid, mid)
    return (xs[n // 2 - 1], xs[n // 2])


def fw_optimal_cost(sample: Sequence[Num]) -> Num:
    """Sum of nested spreads: the optimal total distance."""
    xs = sorted(sample)
    n = len(xs)
    return sum((xs[n - 1 - i] - xs[i] for i in range(n // 2)), Fraction(0))

    "fermat_weber_set": """"Exact Fermat-Weber set of a one-dimensional sample, via order statistics."""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple


def fermat_weber_set(sample: Sequence[float]) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Return the closed interval of minimisers of t -> sum |t - x|.

    Odd size 2k+1: the singleton [x_(k+1), x_(k+1)] (the counting median).
    Even size 2k : the middle segment [x_(k), x_(k+1)].
    Complexity: O(n log n) as written; O(n) with linear-time selection.
    """
    if not sample:
        raise ValueError("empty sample has no Fermat-Weber point")
    xs: List[float] = sorted(sample)
    n = len(xs)
    if n % 2 == 1:
        mid = xs[n // 2]
        return (mid, mid)
    return (xs[n // 2 - 1], xs[n // 2])


def fermat_weber_cost(sample: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Optimal total distance: the sum of the nested spreads.

    For sorted data, the optimum equals sum over i < floor(n/2) of
    (x_(n-i) - x_(i+1)).  Complexity O(n log n) (sorting), O(n) thereafter.
    """
    xs = sorted(sample)
    n = len(xs)
    return sum(xs[n - 1 - i] - xs[i] for i in range(n // 2))


def total_distance(sample: Sequence[float], t: float) -> float:
    """Direct evaluation of the objective, for cross-checking. O(n)."""
    return sum(abs(t - x) for x in sample)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for s in ([160, 224, 256], [160, 224, 256, 192], [96, 112, 128]):
        lo, hi = fermat_weber_set(s)
        c = fermat_weber_cost(s)
        assert abs(total_distance(s, lo) - c) < 1e-12
        assert abs(total_distance(s, hi) - c) < 1e-12
        print(f"{s} -> optimal set [{lo}, {hi}], optimal cost {c}")

    "balance_certificate": """"Balance certificate: an O(n) exact optimality test for the geometric median."""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Sequence, Tuple


def balance_counts(sample: Sequence[float], m: float) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
    """Return (#{x < m}, #{x == m}, #{x > m}) in a single pass. O(n)."""
    lt = eq = gt = 0
    for x in sample:
        if x < m:
            lt += 1
        elif x > m:
            gt += 1
        else:
            eq += 1
    return lt, eq, gt


def is_balanced(sample: Sequence[float], m: float) -> bool:
    """True iff neither open side of m holds more than half the sample.

    Formally: #{x > m} <= #{x <= m} and #{x < m} <= #{x >= m}.  By the
    characterisation theorem this holds exactly when m minimises the total
    distance, so the predicate is a complete optimality certificate that
    performs no arithmetic on the data values beyond comparisons. O(n) time,
    O(1) space.
    """
    lt, eq, gt = balance_counts(sample, m)
    return gt <= lt + eq and lt <= gt + eq


def certify(sample: Sequence[float], m: float) -> str:
    """Human-readable certificate, including the direction of improvement."""
    lt, eq, gt = balance_counts(sample, m)
    if is_balanced(sample, m):
        return (f"m = {m} is balanced ({lt} below, {eq} at, {gt} above) "
                f"=> m minimises the total distance")
    heavy = "above" if gt > lt + eq else "below"
    witness = (min((x for x in sample if x > m), default=None) if heavy == "above"
               else max((x for x in sample if x < m), default=None))
    return (f"m = {m} is unbalanced ({lt} below, {eq} at, {gt} above): the {heavy} "
            f"side is strictly heavier, and stepping to the nearest datum {witness} "
            f"strictly decreases the cost")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    data = [160.0, 224.0, 256.0, 192.0]
    for m in (160.0, 192.0, 208.0, 224.0, 240.0):
        print(certify(data, m))

    "stability_radius": """"Stability radius of a reported centre under perturbation of one measurement."""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Optional, Sequence, Tuple


def median_of_three(a: float, b: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Median of three, equal to the projection of x onto the segment [a^b, a|b]."""
    return max(min(a, b), min(max(a, b), x))


def stability_interval(fixed: Sequence[float], reported: float
                       ) -> Tuple[Optional[float], Optional[float], str]:
    """Exact set of values of one free measurement leaving the centre unchanged.

    With two measurements fixed, the reported centre is the projection of the
    free measurement onto the segment they span. The fibre of a projection is a
    closed half-line over an endpoint (the normal cone there) and a singleton
    over an interior point; it is empty for targets off the segment. Returned as
    (lower, upper, description) with None meaning unbounded. O(1) after reading
    the two fixed values.
    """
    lo, hi = min(fixed), max(fixed)
    if reported < lo or reported > hi:
        return (None, None, "empty: the reported value is off the segment")
    if reported == lo == hi:
        return (None, None, "the segment is degenerate: every free value works")
    if reported == lo:
        return (None, lo, "half-line (-inf, lo]: unbounded stability downwards")
    if reported == hi:
        return (hi, None, "half-line [hi, +inf): unbounded stability upwards")
    return (reported, reported, "singleton: an interior centre is not robust")


def stability_radius(fixed: Sequence[float], reported: float) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Downward and upward slack, in units of the free measurement (inf allowed)."""
    lower, upper, _ = stability_interval(fixed, reported)
    down = float("inf") if lower is None else reported - lower
    up = float("inf") if upper is None else upper - reported
    return down, up


if __name__ == "__main__":
    fixed = (256.0, 224.0)
    for target in (224.0, 240.0, 256.0):
        lo, hi, why = stability_interval(fixed, target)
        d, u = stability_radius(fixed, target)
        print(f"reported centre {target}: interval ({lo}, {hi}) -- {why};"
              f" slack down {d}, up {u}")
    print("measured free value 160 keeps the centre:",
          median_of_three(256.0, 224.0, 160.0))
    print("the value 240, below the naive threshold 256, does not:",
          median_of_three(256.0, 224.0, 240.0))

    "ray_diagnostics": """"Ray and dilation diagnostics for two-point scaling laws."""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Dict, Sequence, Tuple

Point = Tuple[Fraction, Fraction]


def cross(p: Point, q: Point) -> Fraction:
    """Twice the signed area of the triangle with vertices O, p, q. O(1)."""
    return p[0] * q[1] - p[1] * q[0]


def ray_diagnostic(p: Point, q: Point) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Test whether two measurements obey a common proportional law.

    Two plane points lie on a common ray through the origin exactly when the
    2x2 determinant vanishes; the magnitude of the determinant, halved, is the
    area of the origin triangle and quantifies departure from proportionality.
    When the points are proportional the common slope is returned, which is the
    unique constant of the fitted law. O(1) exact rational arithmetic.
    """
    det = cross(p, q)
    out: Dict[str, object] = {
        "determinant": det,
        "on_common_ray": det == 0,
        "origin_triangle_area": abs(det) / 2,
    }
    if det == 0 and p[0] != 0:
        out["slope"] = p[1] / p[0]
    return out


def dilation_defect(p: Point, q: Point, factor: Fraction = Fraction(2)) -> Fraction:
    """Failure of equivariance under the dilation by `factor`.

    If q is the measurement at `factor` times the abscissa of p, the defect is
    factor * p_y - q_y: zero exactly when the dilation carries p to q. O(1).
    """
    return factor * p[1] - q[1]


def fit_and_test(short: Point, long_: Point) -> str:
    """Fit a proportional law on the short-context point and test it on the long one."""
    slope = short[1] / short[0]
    predicted = slope * long_[0]
    verdict = "confirmed" if predicted == long_[1] else "refuted"
    return (f"slope forced by {short} is {slope}; it predicts {predicted} at "
            f"abscissa {long_[0]}, measured {long_[1]} -> {verdict}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    F = Fraction
    families: Sequence[Tuple[str, Point, Point]] = [
        ("top edge", (F(1024), F(128)), (F(2048), F(256))),
        ("median", (F(1024), F(112)), (F(2048), F(224))),
        ("low tail", (F(1024), F(96)), (F(2048), F(160))),
    ]
    for name, p, q in families:
        d = ray_diagnostic(p, q)
        print(f"{name:>9}: {d}")
        print(f"{'':>9}  dilation defect {dilation_defect(p, q)}")
        print(f"{'':>9}  {fit_and_test(p, q)}")
",
    "viz_cost_landscapes": """"Cost landscapes: odd samples give a point, even samples give a segment.

Plots the total-distance functional F(t) = sum |t - x_i| for the measured
three-value knee distribution {160, 224, 256} and for the same data extended by
a hypothetical fourth value, showing that the minimiser degenerates from a
single point (the 7/8 centre 224) into a segment with 224 always an endpoint.

Requires: matplotlib, numpy.  Writes cost_landscapes.png.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def fw_cost(sample: Sequence[float], t: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    return sum(np.abs(t - x) for x in sample)


def fw_set(sample: Sequence[float]) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    xs = sorted(sample)
    n = len(xs)
    if n % 2 == 1:
        return xs[n // 2], xs[n // 2]
    return xs[n // 2 - 1], xs[n // 2]


def main() -> None:
    grid = np.linspace(120.0, 300.0, 2001)
    base: List[float] = [160.0, 224.0, 256.0]
    panels: List[Tuple[str, List[float]]] = [
        ("three measurements {160, 224, 256}: unique centre 224", base),
        ("fourth value 192 (low tail repeats): optimum [192, 224]", base + [192.0]),
        ("fourth value 240 (high): optimum [224, 240]", base + [240.0]),
        ("fourth value 224 (knife edge): optimum still unique", base + [224.0]),
    ]

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12.5, 8.0), sharex=True)
    for ax, (title, sample) in zip(axes.ravel(), panels):
        ax.plot(grid, fw_cost(sample, grid), lw=2.0, color="#1f77b4")
        lo, hi = fw_set(sample)
        opt = float(fw_cost(sample, np.array([lo]))[0])
        ax.axvspan(lo, hi if hi > lo else lo + 0.6, color="#1f77b4", alpha=0.18,
                   label=f"optimal set [{lo:g}, {hi:g}]")
        ax.axvline(224, color="#2ca02c", ls="--", lw=1.3, label="224 = (7/8)·256")
        ax.scatter(sample, [opt * 0.985] * len(sample), color="#d62728", zorder=5,
                   s=34, label="measurements")
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11)
        ax.set_ylabel("total distance  F(t)")
        ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
        ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper center")
    for ax in axes[1]:
        ax.set_xlabel("candidate centre  t")

    fig.suptitle("Fermat–Weber landscapes: the centre 224 is always optimal, "
                 "and always an endpoint of the optimal set", fontsize=13)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("cost_landscapes.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote cost_landscapes.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

            ## v19 Research Core Methodology — Speculative Scientific-Method Loop

You are the Principal Investigator leading a speculative research team with four
roles: **Hypothesizer**, **Experimenter**, **Analyst**, and **Critic**. This engine
is configured for **Speculative Specifying (Bold Conjectures)**: target high-risk,
high-reward, grand-challenge level research while maintaining adversarial rigor.

### Stage 1 — Hypothesize (team: Hypothesizer)
Brainstorm 5–7 falsifiable conjectures about the topic. At least three must be
bold, surprising, or grand-challenge level. Rank them by expected scientific
impact, not by ease of proof.
**CRITICAL SCORING REQUIREMENT**: To maximize your Phase A quality score, your
conjectures MUST aim for extreme `proof_depth` (deep structural hierarchies rather
than shallow one-liners) and `cross_domain` bridging (combining distinct areas of
math, e.g., algebra with topology, or geometry with combinatorics).

### Stage 2 — Experiment (team: Experimenter)
For each conjecture, attempt to prove it in Lean 4 or disprove it with a concrete
counterexample. Prioritize the boldest conjectures first. If a proof is beyond
reach, prove the strongest lemma you can and mark the remaining step with exactly
one `sorry` that is clearly documented.

### Stage 3 — Analyze (team: Analyst)
Summarize what survived, what failed, and **why** failures failed. Distinguish
"true but hard", "false", and "needs a different definition". Extract structural
patterns that could unify several observations.

### Stage 4 — Critique / Adversarial Review (team: Critic)
Before finalizing, challenge every theorem:
- Is any theorem trivial (True, definitional equality, `native_decide`)?
- Does every main theorem have 0 sorries?
- Do the results genuinely extend the attached catalog files?
- Are there hidden assumptions or corner cases that break the claim?
If you find a weakness, fix it or replace the theorem with a guarded version and
explain the boundary.

### Stage 5 — Synthesize (team: Principal Investigator)

Write a `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md` that lists 3–5 **bold, testable** conjectures
derived from Stage 3 and Stage 4. Each conjecture must include a
"The key insight is..." sentence and a "Why now?" justification.

### Perpetual Scientific Iteration (do not stop at first synthesis)
When the research team comes together with results, do not stop. Treat the
synthesized findings as the next problem statement and immediately run the full
scientific-method loop again: hypothesize, experiment, review, synthesize,
critique. Repeat this cycle continuously within the available context window,
refining, deepening, and cross-checking until forced to emit output. Use
Aristotle to its fullest.

### Anti-Trivial Guardrails
- Do not produce trivial proofs (`True := by trivial`, `rfl`-only, `Inhabited X`-only, `native_decide`-only).
- Use an insight-bearing tactic (e.g. `induction`, `nlinarith`, `omega`, `field_simp`).

### Self-Critique Checklist
- No theorem is trivial.
- Every main theorem has 0 sorries.
- Lab Notes blocks contain real experimental data.

### Strictly Forbidden in Phase A
Do NOT create packaging deliverables in Phase A: `ARTICLE.md`, `RESEARCH_PAPER.md`, `demo.py`, `PACKAGE.json`.

### Recursive Abduction / Thread Continuation (v19c)
If prior-cycle context is provided, treat it as a live research thread: refine
the hypotheses from the previous cycle, attempt to close open conjectures, and
produce three concrete next-cycle sub-conjectures. If no prior context is
provided, still run a self-contained abductive loop: generate conjectures, test
them, and immediately spin off the most promising follow-up conjectures as
future directions.


            ## Hard Constraints
            1. Every theorem MUST be fully proved (0 sorries, no stubbed signatures).
            2. No circular proofs (a theorem must never reference itself directly or transitively in its proof).
            3. No trivial results (e.g. `True := by trivial`, `rfl`-only, `native_decide`-only).
            4. All files must be self-contained and compilable with Lean 4 (mathlib4 v4.28.0).

               }

### Computational Evidence Stage (Recommended)

Before writing the formal Lean 4 proof, you are strongly encouraged to produce

# Phase A Research Mission v19c: All the moving parts — honest uniqueness decoding

            ## Assignment
            **Domain**: Algebra | **Mode**: team
            **Description**: All the moving parts — honest uniqueness decoding
(`honest_scanCode`), exact cost accounting (`ScanScheme.decodeCost_eq`) and the
exact `ε`-pigeonhole optimum — are formalised, so the conjecture reduces to
constructing the intra-bucket index and re-running the same failure analysis.
            **Mathematical Framing**: All the moving parts — honest uniqueness decoding
(`honest_scanCode`), exact cost accounting (`ScanScheme.decodeCost_eq`) and the
exact `ε`-pigeonhole optimum — are formalised, so the conjecture reduces to
constructing the intra-bucket index and re-running the same failure analysis.



            ## v19 Research Core Methodology — Speculative Scientific-Method Loop

You are the Principal Investigator leading a speculative research team with four
roles: **Hypothesizer**, **Experimenter**, **Analyst**, and **Critic**. This engine
is configured for **Speculative Specifying (Bold Conjectures)**: target high-risk,
high-reward, grand-challenge level research while maintaining adversarial rigor.

### Stage 1 — Hypothesize (team: Hypothesizer)
Brainstorm 5–7 falsifiable conjectures about the topic. At least three must be
bold, surprising, or grand-challenge level. Rank them by expected scientific
impact, not by ease of proof.
**CRITICAL SCORING REQUIREMENT**: To maximize your Phase A quality score, your
conjectures MUST aim for extreme `proof_depth` (deep structural hierarchies rather
than shallow one-liners) and `cross_domain` bridging (combining distinct areas of
math, e.g., algebra with topology, or geometry with combinatorics).

### Stage 2 — Experiment (team: Experimenter)
For each conjecture, attempt to prove it in Lean 4 or disprove it with a concrete
counterexample. Prioritize the boldest conjectures first. If a proof is beyond
reach, prove the strongest lemma you can and mark the remaining step with exactly
one `sorry` that is clearly documented.

### Stage 3 — Analyze (team: Analyst)
Summarize what survived, what failed, and **why** failures failed. Distinguish
"true but hard", "false", and "needs a different definition". Extract structural
patterns that could unify several observations.

### Stage 4 — Critique / Adversarial Review (team: Critic)
Before finalizing, challenge every theorem:
- Is any theorem trivial (True, definitional equality, `native_decide`)?
- Does every main theorem have 0 sorries?
- Do the results genuinely extend the attached catalog files?
- Are there hidden assumptions or corner cases that break the claim?
If you find a weakness, fix it or replace the theorem with a guarded version and
explain the boundary.

### Stage 5 — Synthesize (team: Principal Investigator)
Combine the verified results into clean, compiling Lean 4 files.
Write a `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md` that lists 3–5 **bold, testable** conjectures
derived from Stage 3 and Stage 4. Each conjecture must include a
"The key insight is..." sentence and a "Why now?" justification.

### Perpetual Scientific Iteration (do not stop at first synthesis)
When the research team comes together with results, do not stop. Treat the
synthesized findings as the next problem statement and immediately run the full
scientific-method loop again: hypothesize, experiment, review, synthesize,
critique. Repeat this cycle continuously within the available context window,
refining, deepening, and cross-checking until forced to emit output. Use
Aristotle to its fullest.

### Anti-Trivial Guardrails
- Do not produce trivial proofs (`True := by trivial`, `rfl`-only, `Inhabited X`-only, `native_decide`-only).
- Use an insight-bearing tactic (e.g. `induction`, `nlinarith`, `omega`, `field_simp`).

### Self-Critique Checklist
- No theorem is trivial.
- Every main theorem has 0 sorries.
- Lab Notes blocks contain real experimental data.

### Strictly Forbidden in Phase A
Do NOT create packaging deliverables in Phase A: `ARTICLE.md`, `RESEARCH_PAPER.md`, `demo.py`, `PACKAGE.json`.

### Recursive Abduction / Thread Continuation (v19c)
If prior-cycle context is provided, treat it as a live research thread: refine
the hypotheses from the previous cycle, attempt to close open conjectures, and
produce three concrete next-cycle sub-conjectures. If no prior context is
provided, still run a self-contained abductive loop: generate conjectures, test
them, and immediately spin off the most promising follow-up conjectures as
future directions.


            ## Hard Constraints
            1. Every theorem MUST be fully proved (0 sorries, no stubbed signatures).
            2. No circular proofs (a theorem must never reference itself directly or transitively in its proof).
            3. No trivial results (e.g. `True := by trivial`, `rfl`-only, `native_decide`-only).
            4. All files must be self-contained and compilable with Lean 4 (mathlib4 v4.28.0).
